99.title: Facing the House
99.hook: wherever you are, you face the Ka'ba in Mecca
99.howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'ba in Mecca for every prayer; mosques mark the direction with a niche called the mihrab, and many people use a compass or a phone app when they pray away from home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taharah, cleanness of body, clothes and place, the half of faith that comes before the prayer. Your line was a clean corner.

A hotel room in Istanbul. On the ceiling above the bed, or on a little sticker by the desk, there's an arrow. It isn't pointing to the exit. In Chicago, someone opens a prayer app, and a compass needle swings and settles. In a mosque, there's a niche in one wall, the mihrab, and every line of people stands facing it. Starting points all over the earth, all turning toward one small building in one valley.
screen: `AN ARROW IN A HOTEL ROOM.` → `A NICHE IN THE WALL.` → `ALL FACING ONE BUILDING.`

segments.voice: The word is qiblah, the direction a person faces in prayer, from a root meaning to face, to be in front of. The qiblah is the Ka'ba, the cube-shaped House in Mecca that the Qur'an says Ibrahim and Isma'il raised. But it wasn't always. A hadith in Bukhari says that after the move to Medina, for sixteen or seventeen months, the Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem. Then, the Qur'an says in Surah al-Baqarah, the Prophet ﷺ kept turning his face toward the sky, and the verse came: turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. The hadith collections tell what happened next. A man who had prayed with the Prophet passed a mosque where people were mid-prayer, still facing Jerusalem, and told them. They turned around, right there in the prayer, to face Mecca. A mosque in Medina is still called the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs. Underneath is an idea from earlier in the same surah: the East and the West belong to Allah, and wherever you turn, there is His face. So Muslims don't say God lives in the Ka'ba. The direction isn't about where God is. It's about where the people are pointed, so a worshipper in Jakarta and one in Lagos stand in the same line. One honest wrinkle. From North America, people work out the direction two ways. Along the shortest path over the curve of the globe, Mecca is to the northeast. Along a straight line on a flat map, it's to the southeast. Communities have followed each, and both are trying to face the same House.
screen: `QIBLAH — THE DIRECTION YOU FACE.` · `FIRST JERUSALEM, THEN MECCA.` · `THEY TURNED IN THE MIDDLE OF PRAYER.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, HIS FACE.` · then, large: `ONE DIRECTION, ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Find the qiblah from where you are, with a compass or a phone app, or roughly: Mecca is in western Arabia, so from Europe it's southeast, from India west, and from North America northeast or southeast, depending on the method your community follows. Turn your body that way and sit still for a moment, picturing the lines of people all over the earth facing the same point you are. If you pray, this is where you'd face.
Qiblah. The direction of prayer, toward the Ka'ba in Mecca, turned from Jerusalem in the Prophet's time. Today's word.
Your line: all turned one way. Starting points all over the earth, and one House. Day ninety-nine, done.

100.title: The five times
100.hook: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, night, and how the sun sets the clock
100.howItsDone: Muslims pray five obligatory prayers a day, fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib and isha, at times set by the sun's position, and, because the times shift daily, they often check a printed timetable or an app.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the qiblah, the direction of prayer, toward the Ka'ba, turned from Jerusalem in the Prophet's time. Your line was all turned one way.

Day one hundred, and a day with five doors in it. The first opens while it's still dark, when the sky just starts to gray. The second, just after the sun passes its highest point. The third, in the long afternoon, when shadows stretch. The fourth, right after the sun disappears. The fifth, when the last red light has gone from the sky. You don't need a clock to find them. You need a window.
screen: `DAY ONE HUNDRED.` → `A DAY WITH FIVE DOORS.` → `YOU NEED A WINDOW, NOT A CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an says, in Surah an-Nisa, that prayer is enjoined on the believers at fixed times. The five are named from the day itself. Fajr, dawn: from first light until sunrise. Dhuhr, midday: just after the sun passes its peak. Asr, afternoon: when a thing's shadow has grown to its own length, or in the Hanafi school, twice its length. Maghrib, sunset: once the sun is gone. And Isha, night: when the twilight has faded. That's why prayer times change every day, and why a timetable in Oslo looks nothing like one in Nairobi. The sun keeps the clock, not the watch. Why five? A hadith in Bukhari tells it as part of the Night Journey. On the ascent, the Prophet ﷺ was given fifty prayers a day. On his way down, Musa stopped him and said, in effect, your people won't manage that, go back and ask for less. He went back again and again, and it came down to five. The hadith ends: five in the doing, fifty in the reward. Look where the times fall: waking, the middle of work, the afternoon slump, the end of the day, the edge of sleep. Five hinges of an ordinary day, and a prayer at each. Shia practice allows joining them into three sittings, dawn, midday with afternoon, sunset with night, and Sunni schools allow joining on a journey. It's still five prayers.

segments.voice: Look up today's five times where you are, from a prayer app, a mosque's website or a search, and read them slowly: fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha. Notice which have passed and which is next, then look out a window if you can and guess where the sun is on that path. If you pray, you can set a small reminder for the next one.
Salah, the obligatory prayer prescribed five times a day: fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha, set by the sun, fifty that became five.
Your line: the sun keeps the times. Five doors, and the light opens each one. One hundred days, and counting.

101.title: Allahu akbar
101.hook: hands raised, the prayer opens, the world is set behind you
101.howItsDone: Every Muslim prayer opens with the takbir: raising the hands to the shoulders or ears and saying Allahu akbar, after which the worshipper stays focused on the prayer, not speaking, eating or turning away, until the closing salam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salah, five prayers from dawn to night, set by the sun, fifty that became five. Your line was the sun keeps the times.

You're washed, facing the right way, and the time has come in. You're standing on a clean spot, your phone still buzzing in your pocket, half your mind on an email you didn't finish. Then the person in front raises both hands, palms forward, up by the ears, and says two words. For the next few minutes, the email doesn't exist. You can't answer the phone. You can't turn to chat. Something has closed behind you like a door.
screen: `WASHED, FACING, ON TIME.` → `BOTH HANDS RAISED.` → `A DOOR CLOSES BEHIND YOU.`

segments.voice: The words are Allahu akbar, and saying them is called takbir. Most people translate them as God is great. But akbar is a comparative, like bigger or greater, so a closer sense is: God is greater. Greater than what? The sentence doesn't say, and that's the point. Greater than the email, the worry, whatever you walked in carrying. Greater than anything you could put at the end of the sentence. The first takbir of the prayer has its own name: takbirat al-ihram, the takbir of making things forbidden. Ihram is the same word used for a pilgrim's sacred state. Once it's said, ordinary things become off-limits: eating, talking, looking around, anything that isn't the prayer. A hadith in the Sunan collections puts the whole prayer in one sentence: its key is purity, its opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam. So the cleanness from day ninety-eight is the key, and today's words turn it. Then the hands. Most Muslims raise them to the shoulders or to the ears; the schools of law describe it a little differently, and all of them are doing the same thing. Many teachers describe it as throwing the world behind you. And takbir doesn't stay in the prayer. It's in the call to prayer, it's said when a baby is born, on the Eid mornings, on a hilltop. It marks every change of position in the prayer, as you'll hear over the next few days: the hinge the whole prayer turns on.
screen: `AKBAR — NOT GREAT, GREATER.` · `THE TAKBIR THAT FORBIDS.` · `ITS OPENING IS THE TAKBIR.` · `THE WORLD SET BEHIND YOU.` · then, large: `GREATER THAN ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: Stand, if you can, and think of the one thing tugging at you most right now; name it silently. Then raise both hands, palms forward, to your shoulders or your ears, and if you pray, say it once, quietly, Allahu akbar; if not, just notice the feeling of setting something behind you. Lower your hands, and let the next two minutes be empty of that thing.
Takbir. Saying Allahu akbar, God is greater: the opening of the prayer, the door that closes behind you. Today's word.
Your line: greater than all of it. Whatever feels like the biggest thing in the room, the sentence stays open. That's day one hundred one.

102.title: Standing and reciting
102.hook: you stand and recite al-Fatiha, then a short surah
102.howItsDone: In each unit of prayer, Muslims stand and recite al-Fatiha in Arabic, adding another passage of the Qur'an in the first two units; at dawn, sunset and night the leader recites the first two units aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday: takbir, Allahu akbar, God is greater: hands raised, and the prayer opened. Your line was greater than all of it.

The hands come down. In some schools, they fold over the body; in others, they rest at the sides. The eyes drop to the spot where the forehead will touch the ground. And then, for the first time in the prayer, the person speaks at length. Not a speech. Not a list of requests. A short chapter you first met in this path's first week, the one that asks for directions. Standing still, in front of no one you can see, saying it as if someone is listening.
screen: `THE HANDS COME DOWN.` → `EYES ON THE PLACE OF PROSTRATION.` → `THEN THE FIRST WORDS.`

segments.voice: The standing is called qiyam, from a root meaning to stand up, to rise, to stand firm. In it, every unit of the prayer begins with al-Fatiha, the Opening. A hadith in Bukhari is blunt about it: there's no prayer for the one who doesn't recite the Opening of the Book. So it comes back in every unit of every prayer. It begins, in Pickthall's translation: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." And at its center: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help." Now the surprise. A hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet ﷺ relays words from God, says the prayer is divided between God and the one praying. When the person says, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, God says: My servant has praised Me. At the Beneficent, the Merciful: My servant has extolled Me. And at the middle line: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant will have what he asks. So in the tradition's own telling, the standing isn't a recital into empty air. It's a conversation, answered line by line. After the Fatiha, in the first two units, the person adds some other part of the Qur'an, often a short surah from the end of the book, like al-Ikhlas, four lines long. At dawn, sunset and night, the first two units are recited aloud by the one leading; at midday and afternoon, silently.

segments.voice: Stand still, feet a little apart, hands folded or at your sides, eyes resting on a spot on the floor in front of you. If you know the Fatiha, recite it slowly, leaving a small pause after each line, as if waiting for the answer. If you don't know it, say just its first line in Pickthall's translation, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, and stand in the quiet after it.
Qiyam. The standing in prayer, where the Fatiha is recited, then a short surah. Today's word.
Your line: stand and speak. In the hadith's telling, every line is answered. Day one hundred two, done.

103.title: The bow
103.hook: back straight, hands on knees, glory to my Lord the Great
103.howItsDone: After reciting, Muslims say Allahu akbar and bow with hands on their knees and back level, usually saying subhana rabbiya al-'azim three times, and remaining still in the bow before rising.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qiyam, the standing, where the Fatiha is recited and, in the hadith's telling, answered line by line. Your line was stand and speak.

A man walks into the mosque in Medina and prays, quickly. Then he comes over to the Prophet ﷺ and greets him with salaam. The Prophet returns the greeting, and then says something the man didn't expect: go back and pray, because you haven't prayed. In a bow, the body can look finished before it has arrived. A dip of the head and shoulders, and it's over. So what was that man missing?
screen: `A MAN PRAYS QUICKLY.` → `HE GREETS THE PROPHET.` → `GO BACK AND PRAY.`

segments.voice: The bow is called ruku', from a root meaning to bend, to bow down. After the recitation, the person says Allahu akbar and bends forward from the hips, hands on the knees, back level, head in line with the back. There, usually three times, they say: subhana rabbiya al-'azim. Glory to my Lord, the Magnificent, the Great. A report in the Sunan says that when a verse came telling the Prophet to glorify the name of his Lord, the Tremendous, he said: put it in your bowing. Now, the man in the mosque. The hadith is in Bukhari. He went back and prayed, came again, and was told again: go back and pray, you haven't prayed. Three times. Finally he said: by the One who sent you with the truth, I don't know any better, so teach me. And the Prophet did. Among the things he said: bow until you are at rest in your bowing. That's the missing piece. There's a word for it, tuma'nina: stillness, settling. The body has to arrive in the bow before it leaves. A bow that's only a dip is a gesture. A bow that settles says, with the whole spine, that the one bowing isn't in a hurry to stand back up. And in the tradition, a Muslim bows like this to God alone. Not to a king, not to a teacher, not to a parent. That's the sense in which the bow is honest: it means what it shows, and it's aimed where the tradition says it belongs.

Your line: bowing is honest. Stillness was the piece the hurried man was missing. See you tomorrow.

104.title: Rising from the bow
104.hook: you rise saying Allah hears whoever praises Him
104.howItsDone: Rising from the bow, the prayer leader says sami'a Allahu liman hamidah, and the congregation, standing straight and still, responds rabbana wa laka al-hamd before going down to prostrate.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ruku', the bow, back level, still enough to be at rest. Your line was bowing is honest.

A message marked read, and no reply. A joke at dinner that lands on nobody. A voicemail that may never be played. A lot of what gets said goes out with no sign of where it lands. In the prayer, the bow is over, and the body comes back up. On the way up, before the person is even straight, the one leading says a sentence about exactly that. Not a request. A statement.
screen: `A MESSAGE MARKED READ.` → `NO REPLY.` → `A SENTENCE ON THE WAY UP.`

segments.voice: Rising from the bow, the one leading the prayer says: sami'a Allahu liman hamidah. Allah hears whoever praises Him. Sami'a means He heard, He hears, with the sense of listening and answering. Then, standing straight, the people answer: rabbana wa laka al-hamd. Our Lord, and to You be the praise. Notice the shape: one voice says God hears, and everyone replies with praise, as if to say, then hear this. The scholars call this standing position i'tidal, straightening, and like the bow, it isn't a pass-through. Yesterday's hadith, the man who prayed too fast, includes it: rise until you are standing straight. Now the story that makes this moment famous. It's in Bukhari, from a companion named Rifa'a ibn Rafi'. One day, praying behind the Prophet ﷺ, a man rose from the bow and, after our Lord and to You be the praise, added a few words of his own: praise, abundant, good and blessed. When the prayer ended, the Prophet asked who had said it. The man said, I did. And the Prophet said he had seen thirty-some angels racing each other to be the first to write it down. One person, one sentence of praise in a line of worshippers, and in the hadith, angels hurry to record it. In the tradition's reading, that is what sami'a Allahu liman hamidah promises: praise doesn't vanish into the room. It is heard.

If you pray, whisper sami'a Allahu liman hamidah as you rise, and, standing, rabbana wa laka al-hamd. If you don't, just notice the moment of arriving upright, and stay there, straight and still, for three breaths before you sit.

Your line: he hears. In the hadith, even one added sentence had angels racing. That's one hundred four.

105.title: The prostration
105.hook: forehead on the ground, glory to my Lord the Most High, the closest a person gets
105.howItsDone: In each unit of prayer, Muslims prostrate twice on seven points (forehead and nose, hands, knees, toes), usually saying subhana rabbiya al-a'la three times, and some add their own supplications there silently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: i'tidal, rising from the bow: Allah hears whoever praises Him. Your line was he hears. This week: a direction to face, five times set by the sun, two words that close a door, standing and being answered, a bow that settles, rising and being heard.

Knees, then hands, then the forehead on the floor. The highest part of a person, the part with the face and the mind in it, placed on the same ground you walk on. In a wrestling match, ending up face-down is losing. In the prayer, it's the moment of nearness. Every day this week the body has gone a little lower. Now it goes all the way down.
screen: `KNEES, HANDS, FOREHEAD.` → `ON THE GROUND YOU WALK ON.` → `NOW ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: The word is sujud, prostration. The same root gives masjid, the Arabic word behind mosque: the place of prostration. The whole building is named for this one moment. A hadith in Bukhari says it's done on seven bones: the forehead, with the nose; the two hands; the two knees; and the toes of both feet. Seven points of the body touching the earth, and every unit of the prayer has two prostrations. There, usually three times, the person says: subhana rabbiya al-a'la. Glory to my Lord, the Most High. Notice the pairing. In the bow, you said the Great. Now, at the lowest point your body can reach, you say the Most High. The lower you go, the higher the name. Then the hadith that gives today its line, in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet ﷺ said: the closest a servant is to his Lord is while prostrating, so make much supplication there. Not standing tall. Not at the head of a line. Face on the floor. The hadith points there for a person's own requests, said silently. Surah al-Alaq, the surah that begins with Read, ends on the same idea: prostrate yourself, and draw near. In the hadith, the lowest point is the nearest.
screen: `SUJUD — THE MASJID IS NAMED FOR IT.` · `SEVEN BONES ON THE EARTH.` · `GLORY TO MY LORD, THE MOST HIGH.` · `THE CLOSEST A SERVANT IS.` · then, large: `PROSTRATE, AND DRAW NEAR.`

segments.voice: If your body allows, kneel, place your hands flat on the floor, and lower your forehead and nose to the ground; if it doesn't, sit and bow your head as low as is comfortable, and that counts too. Stay there, and feel the seven points, or however many are touching. If you pray, you can say subhana rabbiya al-a'la three times, then ask for one thing in your own words, and rest there.
Sujud. Prostration: forehead on the ground, glory to my Lord the Most High, the closest a person gets. Today's word.
Your line: closest when lowest. Brought low, in the tradition's hearing, might be the closest place. A week of the prayer, done.
